history.alt_text: Towering robotic warehouse storage racks with orange shuttle robots, receding in compressed rows toward an unfinished concrete bay.
history.caption: The decade's warehouse automation is already sold — racked, booked and waiting to be built.
history.title: Pre-sold automation racks receding to an unfinished bay

style_when: scale is the story — a port, a refinery, a data centre hall, a rail yard, a skyline of cranes — and the reader needs to feel how big it is
prompt: 200mm telephoto photograph inside a vast distribution warehouse aisle, flat compressed perspective stacking row upon row of towering high-bay aluminum storage racks — Symbotic-style automation — densely slotted with grey totes, weathered-orange autonomous shuttle robots climbing the rail tracks inside the rack bays. Hard directional daylight from high skylights upper-left, raking across rack faces into long deep shadows down the polished concrete aisle; graphite and charcoal steel, safety-yellow floor lines, weathered orange, fine film grain. No people anywhere. At the far right the last rack row meets bare concrete where palletized steel beams wait unassembled. Extreme asymmetry: the rack system commands the left two-thirds, rows compressing toward the shadowed unfinished bay, gentle lens falloff.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, numbers, logos, watermark
rationale: The story's protagonist is the warehouse robotics system itself, already sold at $22.3 billion scale, so the machine must command the frame in its real environment. Telephoto compression is the one optic that makes backlog feel physical — rack rows stacking into the distance like contracted years — and the unstaffed, half-built hall carries the workforce tension without a single figure.
subject: towering warehouse automation racks with climbing shuttle robots inside a distribution center, receding toward bare unfinished floor
core_thesis: A decade of warehouse automation has already been sold — Symbotic's $22.3 billion backlog is booked robot work signed before the labor cuts it was priced against ever land.
core_conflict: Robot payback cases built on ever-rising wage inflation versus a labor line now shrinking by plan (P&G's 20–30% cut) — once headcount falls on schedule the savings stop compounding while the capital is still owed, with nearly half of all booked work riding on a single buyer.
composition: extreme asymmetry — the rack-and-robot system commands the left two-thirds, its rows compressing toward a shadowed unfinished bay at the right
alt_text: Tall robotic storage racks with orange shuttle robots receding down a warehouse aisle, with no people in sight.
caption: The backlog sells the next decade of robot work forward while buyers commit to smaller supply staffs.
title: Automation'S Next Decade Is Already Sold

review.depicts: Tall multi-level warehouse storage racks filled with orange and gray robotic shuttle vehicles inside a distribution center, the rack rows receding toward a bare, empty concrete floor on the right side of the frame.
review.reason: The frame depicts the article's own protagonist and mechanism — warehouse automation racks with shuttle robots, exactly Symbotic's product — and the bare unfinished floor at right visually echoes the booked-but-not-yet-delivered backlog the headline references.
